working: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (1 + 2i sin t): the quotient becomes ((3 - 4 sin^2 t) + 8i sin t)/(1 + 4 sin^2 t). It is real exactly when 8 sin t = 0, i.e. sin t = 0. working: Write a = e^(i alpha), b = e^(i beta), c = e^(i gamma), each of unit modulus. Then b/c + c/a + a/b = e^(i(beta-gamma)) + e^(i(gamma-alpha)) + e^(i(alpha-beta)), whose imaginary part is exactly sin(beta-gamma) + sin(gamma-alpha) + sin(alpha-beta) — the same sum the question asks for, just reordered. (1+i)^n/(1-i)^(n-2) = [(1+i)/(1-i)]^n * (1-i)^2. Since (1+i)/(1-i) = i and (1-i)^2 = -2i, the expression equals i^n * (-2i) = -2 i^(n+1). Evaluated both sides for n = 1,2,3,4,5,7,10,-3: option C matched at every value while A, B and D failed (e.g. n=1 gives 2, and -2 i^2 = 2, whereas -i^0 = -1).

working: The line x = 4y - 2 is y = (x+2)/4 and the parabola is y = x^2/4. Setting them equal gives x^2 = x + 2, so x = -1 and x = 2. Area = (1/4) * integral from -1 to 2 of (x + 2 - x^2) dx = (1/4)(9/2) = 9/8. Confirmed by numeric integration over 2,000,000 strips: 1.1250000.

working: From the shared context alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha*beta = c/a. For a^3 x^2 + abc x + c^3 = 0 the root sum is -bc/a^2 and the product is c^3/a^3. alpha + beta = -b/a = sin t + cos t and alpha*beta = c/a = sin t cos t. Squaring the first, b^2/a^2 = 1 + 2c/a, so b^2 = a^2 + 2ac. Then b^2 + c^2 = a^2 + 2ac + c^2 = (a+c)^2, which is option D. Tested numerically at three awkward angles (t = 0.37, 1.13, 2.90 rad) and with a = 2.7 as well as a = 1: D held to machine precision every time, while A, B and C each failed.
notes: with sin(theta) and cos(theta) as the roots of ax^2+bx+c, the sum is -b/a and the product c/a. Squaring the sum: b^2/a^2 = 1 + 2c/a, so b^2 = a^2 + 2ac. Then (a+c)^2 = a^2 + 2ac + c^2 = b^2 + c^2, which is option D. Option A fails unless c = 2a, so it is not an identity

working: Since a*alpha^2 + b*alpha + c = 0, alpha(a*alpha + b) = -c, so 1/(a*alpha + b) = -alpha/c, and likewise for beta. Sum of the new roots = -(alpha+beta)/c = b/(ac); product = alpha*beta/c^2 = 1/(ac). The monic equation x^2 - (b/ac)x + 1/(ac) = 0 clears to ac*x^2 - bx + 1 = 0, which is option A. Verified by computing 1/(a*alpha+b), 1/(a*beta+b) directly for (a,b,c) = (2,-5,3), (1,7,5), (3,2,-4) and matching them against the roots of each option — A matched all three, B gave the negatives, C gave unrelated values.

From x^2 - px - q = 0: u + v = p and uv = -q. I is correct — reversing the coefficients gives -q x^2 - p x + 1 = 0, i.e. q x^2 + p x - 1 = 0, whose root sum -p/q equals (u+v)/(uv) and whose root product -1/q equals 1/(uv). II is correct — (x-p)(x+q) = 0 has roots p and -q, which are precisely u+v and uv. III is FALSE — the equation with roots u^2, v^2 is x^2 - (p^2+2q)x + q^2 = 0, not x^2 + p^2 x + q^2 = 0, since u^2 + v^2 = p^2 + 2q, not -p^2. Checked with (p,q) = (1,1), (3,-2), (-4,5): I and II matched every time, III never did (e.g. p=3,q=-2 gives u^2,v^2 = 1,4 while the stated equation has roots -8.53 and -0.47).

INDRAPRASTHA has 12 letters: A x3, R x2, and I, N, D, P, S, T, H once each. Vowels never separated means the four vowels I,A,A,A form one block. The 8 consonants (with R twice) plus the block give 9!/2! = 181440 arrangements, and the block's internal order gives 4!/3! = 4. Total 181440 x 4 = 725760.

Leading digit must be 3,4,5 or 6 (4 ways) and each of the other three places is free among the six digits: 4 x 6^3 = 864. Confirmed by exhaustively enumerating all 6^4 strings and counting those > 3000 (864). Option D, 1296 = 6^4, is the count with no lower bound at all.

working: Put t = log10 x and take log10 of both sides (valid and order-preserving for x > 0): t(t^2 - 3t + 1) > 3, i.e. t^3 - 3t^2 + t - 3 > 0, which factors as (t-3)(t^2+1) > 0. Since t^2+1 > 0 always, this needs t > 3, i.e. x > 1000. working: Expanding the determinant, the middle term vanishes (-sin(t)+sin(t) = 0) and the other two give (1+sin^2 t) + (sin^2 t + 1), so det A = 2 + 2 sin^2 t; sympy confirms 2*sin(theta)**2 + 2. For a 3x3 matrix adj(adj A) = |A|^(n-2) A = |A| A. Here |A| = 1(24-24) - 2(16-20) + 3(12-15) = 8 - 9 = -1, so adj(adj A) = -A. Verified in sympy: adj(adj A) computes to [[-1,-2,-3],[-2,-3,-4],[-5,-6,-8]], exactly -A.

Each adjoint squares the determinant of a 3x3 matrix, so four applications give |A|^(2^4) = |A|^16. Since |A| = -1, this is (-1)^16 = 1. Confirmed in sympy by taking the adjugate four times in succession: the determinant is 1 after every step. The powers-of-two options are built for a matrix with |A| = 2 and do not apply here.

working: A*A^T has diagonal entries cos^2(t)+sin^2(t)=1 and off-diagonal entries cos(t)sin(t)-sin(t)cos(t)=0, so A*A^T=I and A is orthogonal. det A = 1 (non-zero) rules out nilpotent; A^2 is the rotation through 2t, which equals neither I nor A for general t, ruling out involutory and idempotent.

Multiply A^3 - 6A^2 + 5A + 11I = 0 through by A^{-1}: A^2 - 6A + 5I + 11A^{-1} = 0, so A^{-1} = -(1/11)(A^2 - 6A + 5I). Computing A^2 = [[4,2,1],[-3,8,-14],[7,-3,14]] gives A^2 - 6A + 5I = [[3,-4,-5],[-9,1,4],[-5,3,1]], hence A^{-1} = (1/11)[[-3,4,5],[9,-1,-4],[5,-3,-1]]. Verified by multiplying A into each option: only (A) returns I (max residual 6e-42); B, C, D are off by 1.91, 0.91, 4.45. (The stated identity is just Cayley-Hamilton: trace 6, sum of principal 2x2 minors 5, det -11.)

working: I is true: (A^2)^T = (A^T)^2 = (-A)^2 = A^2, so A^2 is symmetric. II is true: skew-symmetry forces a_ii = -a_ii, so every diagonal entry is 0 and the trace vanishes for ANY order, odd included. Both statements hold.

working: The coefficient determinant |[[1,2,3],[2,1,3],[1,1,2]]| = 1(2-3) - 2(4-3) + 3(2-1) = -1 - 2 + 3 = 0, so there is no unique solution. Row-reducing the augmented matrix: R2-2R1 = [0,-3,-3 | 0] and R3-R1 = [0,-1,-1 | 2]; the two left-hand sides are proportional while the right-hand sides are not, forcing 0 = 2. The system is inconsistent, so it has no solution.

working: |x^2 sin(1/x)| <= x^2, so by squeeze lim_{x->0} f(x) = 0 and the limit exists. f'(0) = lim_{h->0} (h^2 sin(1/h))/h = lim h sin(1/h) = 0 by the same squeeze, so the derivative at 0 exists too - hence (C). (D) is false: for x != 0, f'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x), and cos(1/x) has no limit as x->0, so f' is not continuous at 0.

subtopic: Continuity and Differentiability — Piecewise, Modulus, Composed, Oscillatory
working: sin(x^2)/x = x * (sin(x^2)/x^2) -> 0*1 = 0 = f(0), so f is continuous at 0. f'(0) = lim_{h->0} (sin(h^2)/h)/h = lim sin(h^2)/h^2 = 1, so f is derivable at 0 as well. The conclusion is unchanged under the alternative reading sin^2(x)/x, whose difference quotient is (sin h / h)^2 -> 1. Either way the function is continuous AND derivable.
